subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Sky Dark?
description: A short lesson to help you apply Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Sky Dark?.

hook.text: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, the sky should be bright everywhere. So why is it dark at night?

buildup.text: Heinrich Olbers posed this in 1823. In an infinite, eternal universe, every sightline should end at a star.

discovery.text: The answer is that the universe has a finite age. Light from the most distant stars hasn't reached us yet.

twist.text: Also, the expansion of space stretches distant starlight into invisible infrared and microwave wavelengths.

climax.text: The dark night sky is itself evidence that the universe had a beginning and is expanding. Darkness tells a story.

punchline.text: A dark sky proves the universe isn't infinite or eternal. Darkness speaks.

quiz.question: Why is the night sky dark if there are countless stars?
options: The universe has a finite age, so light from distant stars hasn't reached us yet
Most stars are too dim to be seen from Earth
Interstellar dust blocks nearly all starlight

details.summary: Olbers' paradox asks: if the universe is infinite and filled with stars, why isn't the night sky blazing bright in every direction? The resolution is twofold: the universe has a finite age (so light from distant stars hasn't reached us) and cosmic expansion redshifts distant starlight beyond…
details.whyItMatters: This deceptively simple question — why is the sky dark at night? — turns out to require understanding the Big Bang, the finite age of the universe, and cosmic expansion. A child's question demands modern cosmology to answer.
takeaways: An infinite, static universe would produce a bright night sky
The sky is dark because the universe has a finite age
Cosmic expansion also redshifts distant starlight to invisibility

faq.question: Who first posed Olbers' paradox?
faq.answer: Although named after Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers (1823), the puzzle was discussed earlier by Thomas Digges (1576), Kepler (1610), and others. Olbers popularized it, and his name stuck.

faq.question: Is the sky actually dark in all wavelengths?
faq.answer: No. The cosmic microwave background fills the entire sky with microwave radiation — every direction glows at 2.7 Kelvin. Olbers' paradox is resolved for visible light, but in microwave wavelengths, the sky indeed glows uniformly — the redshifted remnant of a once-bright, hot early universe.
